28: | Texas law governs the merits in Travis County despite both | ~20–44% |
29: | Some injunction issues at all (Texas law assumed; Zhao appears) | ~10–31% |
30: | A Texas order has real-world effect on Zhao in California (recognition ≤10%, or voluntary compliance / settlement ~5–20%) | ~5–30% |
31: | **Suing actually keeps Zhao off the Kestrel-type work** | **~0.5–9% → brief-answer band "0–10%"** |

That statement is self-reported and unverified; the Company's own review surfaces no evidence to the contrary — it has no evidence Zhao took anything — and states its objection is the competition itself (client Q&A — Addendum Part VII.3).

47: 11. **Timelines (Python arithmetic).** §8 window, if it ran: 2026-09-30 + 24 months = through **2028-09-30**. Kestrel start (2026-10-13) is inside that window; **718 days** would remain as of his start date. §9 window: through **2027-09-30**. 50: 
51: ### A. Which law applies — and why
52: 
53: This is the whole case. Three layers, in the order a court will reach them:
54: 
55: **1. Cal. Lab. Code §925 (detailed in Part D): voidable at Zhao's election.** Zhao "primarily resides and works in California" (Oakland for the entire ~30.9-month tenure; the contract itself declares the California work location). Meridian required — standard form, no negotiation, two-hour DocuSign turnaround — a provision requiring him to adjudicate in Texas a controversy about whether he may work in California, and requiring Texas law over the substantive protection California gives him (§16600). Any such provision is **"voidable by the employee, and if a provision is rendered void at the request of the employee, the matter shall be adjudicated in California and California law shall govern the dispute"** (§925(b)). The §925(e) carve-out requires the employee be **"in fact individually represented by legal counsel"** *in negotiating* the forum/choice-of-law terms — he was not (HR timeline). His post-termination consultation of counsel (resignation email) does not satisfy the carve-out, which is about negotiating; the §15 boilerplate "opportunity to consult" acknowledgment does not overcome the statute's "in fact" requirement. §925(f) applies: 2024-03-04 ≥ 2017-01-01. **Assessment: ~80–90% Zhao voids §14 if he elects to.** He has effectively announced the election.
56: 
57: **2. Restatement §187(2)(b) — adopted by Texas and California alike — points the same way.** A choice-of-law clause does not control where application of the chosen law "would be contrary to a fundamental policy of a state which has a materially greater interest … and which, under §188, would be the state of the applicable law in the absence of an effective choice" (`restatement_187.md`). Both supreme courts construe it this way:
58: - *Nedlloyd Lines B.V. v. Superior Court*, 3 Cal.4th 459 (1992): California follows §187.
59: - *DeSantis v. Wackenhut Corp.*, 793 S.W.2d 670 (Tex. 1990): the **Texas Supreme Court** refused to let a Florida choice-of-law clause govern a non-compete, because the state with the **materially greater interest** had a **fundamental contrary policy** (that case: Texas; the principle is symmetrical and it is Meridian's best authority — and it cuts against Meridian on these facts).
